newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian farm coffee prices low despite world spike.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian farm coffee prices low despite world spike.

text.p: Ivorian coffee farmgate prices have not risen despite a world price rally resulting from a supply shortage and low consumer stocks, upcountry buyers said on Wednesday.

"If anything (farmgate) prices are going down. There is plenty of coffee about but no world price (rise) effect on sentiment," said one, adding that exporters were discounting coffee prices by up to 20 percent on grounds of poor quality.

"There was a world price boom 2-3 years ago and a (main Ivorian buyer) bought up about 60-70 percent of the total (Ivorian) crop," said one. "That pushed up prices to farmers but it is not happening this time."
High world prices had not filtered down to Ivorian farmers because buyers were reluctant to pay over the state guide price of 495 CFA a kg, exporters said.
Many growers were being paid a maximum of 425 CFA/kg as buyers passed down quality discounts.
Upcountry buying slackened off after a March peak. Exporters had already built up stocks to meet export contracts before world robusta prices spiked this week.
A slow start to Ivory Coast's marketing season had meant stocks remained in Ivorian warehouses rather than moving into consumer stocks.
Port arrivals totalled around 250,000 tonnes in early May compared to the government's official full-year forecast of 230,000 tonnes.
Unexported warehouse stocks stood at around 120,000 tonnes, port sources estimated this week.
Exports of remaining warehouse stocks are expected to last until the end of September, slightly later than usual.

"The Caistab is in the market every day (for selling export contracts)," said one exporter. "Some of the contracts have been sitting around since April but it (the Caistab) is also selling for August and September."
Exporters said roaster demand was unlikely to affect export prices earned in Ivory Coast.

Local roasters, including Nestle -- which has its own upcountry buying stations -- exported a negligible 694 tonnes of soluble coffee in the first six months of the 1996/97 (October-September) season. Most Ivorian coffee beans are for export.
One trader told Reuters that international roasters had probably substituted as much robusta for arabica as they could without breaking into new product development to stimulate demand.

"The (world) prices will not really have any effect on us," said one manager for SIFCA, a main Ivorian exporter. "People have already bought the coffee so the main problem now is finding the factory capacity for grading it."
Total grading capacity stands at an estimated 20,000 tonnes/month.

Several upcountry sorting plants closed after a world price slump in the early 1990s, but some exporters are planning to raise coffee grading capacity over the next two years by buying or renovating equipment.
The speculative position of Ivorian exporters and the level of European roaster stocks was unclear.

"It is possible to buy export contracts from the Caistab (marketing board) and set up export guarantees without selling directly," said one exporter. "It is a 100 percent risk and depends on your bank agreeing to put money upfront but some people are probably doing it."
